title: Sensitive Data Handling and Audit Trails
learningObjectives: Identify sensitive fields that should not appear in routine query output.
Apply data minimization to SELECT statements.
Create an audit table for security-relevant changes.
Record before-and-after values without exposing unnecessary personal data.
Explain audit access, integrity and retention requirements.

understand.concept: Sensitive-data handling limits what is collected, stored, displayed and retained. Audit trails record who changed what and when so important actions can be investigated.
understand.whyItMatters: A technically correct query can still create a privacy incident if it returns credentials, payment data or unnecessary personal information.
understand.analogy: A visitor log records that a restricted room was entered without publishing the contents of every file in that room.
understand.analogyLimit: An audit table is not tamper-proof merely because it is in a database. Administrators, backups, retention rules and application trust boundaries still matter.

explain.narrative:
## Data minimization
Collect only information needed for a defined purpose. Use explicit column lists instead of SELECT * in sensitive workflows. Mask or omit identifiers in logs and user-facing screens when full values are unnecessary.

## Audit records
An audit record commonly includes an event identifier, subject key, action, timestamp, actor reference and a carefully selected before/after value. Do not copy entire sensitive rows into audit tables without a retention and access plan.

## Integrity and privacy
Restrict audit-table writes and reads, protect logs from unauthorized modification, define retention periods and ensure audit records do not become a second uncontrolled store of personal data. Database triggers can capture changes, but their behaviour and security properties vary by engine.

## Password and payment data
Password verification belongs in a dedicated password-hashing system. Payment card data and secrets require specialized compliance and protection; do not store raw secrets in ordinary application tables or demonstration logs.

examples.title: Create a minimal customer profile table
examples.code: CREATE TABLE sec20_customers (customer_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, display_name TEXT NOT NULL, contact_email TEXT NOT NULL, marketing_opt_in INTEGER NOT NULL CHECK (marketing_opt_in IN (0,1)));
examples.explanation: Stores only a display name, contact email and consent flag for this example. Real systems should define purpose, retention and access rules for each personal-data field.

examples.title: Insert two demonstration customer profiles
examples.explanation: Adds sample profiles with synthetic example.test addresses. Do not use real customer contact details in a public learning database.

examples.title: Return only fields needed for a contact list
examples.code: SELECT customer_id, display_name FROM sec20_customers WHERE marketing_opt_in = 1 ORDER BY customer_id;
examples.explanation: Selects only the identifier and display name for opted-in customers. The contact email is not returned because this particular view does not need it.

examples.title: Create a focused change-audit table
examples.code: CREATE TABLE sec20_customer_audit (audit_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, customer_id INTEGER NOT NULL, field_name TEXT NOT NULL, old_value TEXT, new_value TEXT, actor_ref TEXT NOT NULL, event_time TEXT NOT NULL);
examples.explanation: Stores a targeted field-change record. The audit schema deliberately avoids copying the complete customer row and uses actor_ref rather than storing an authentication secret.

examples.title: Update consent and record the corresponding audit event
examples.code: BEGIN; UPDATE sec20_customers SET marketing_opt_in = 0 WHERE customer_id = 1; INSERT INTO sec20_customer_audit VALUES (1, 1, 'marketing_opt_in', '1', '0', 'admin-17', '2026-11-22T10:00:00Z'); COMMIT; SELECT field_name, old_value, new_value FROM sec20_customer_audit WHERE customer_id = 1;
examples.explanation: Updates the consent flag and inserts a corresponding audit event in the same transaction. In production, capture the actor and timestamp from trusted server context, verify the update affected exactly one row and restrict access to the audit table.

practise.guidedTask: Run the examples and compare the customer list with the audit table. Identify which personal field is intentionally omitted from the list and why the audit stores a narrow field-level change.
practise.independentTask: Design an audit trail for a change to an employee's department. Include actor, event time, subject key and before/after department identifiers. Explain how you would restrict audit reads and define retention.
hints: Use explicit SELECT columns in sensitive workflows.
Do not store plaintext passwords or raw secrets.
Keep audit events narrow and purpose-specific.
Record audit and business changes in one transaction where appropriate.
Define access controls and retention for audit data.

options: Collect and expose only data needed for a defined purpose
Return every column for convenience
Copy every row into an audit table
Keep all data forever
questions.answer: Collect and expose only data needed for a defined purpose
questions.explanation: Minimization reduces privacy exposure and unnecessary retention.

questions.prompt: Why prefer explicit columns to SELECT * in a sensitive report?
options: It avoids exposing fields the report does not need
It disables constraints
It automatically encrypts results
It creates a database backup
questions.answer: It avoids exposing fields the report does not need
questions.explanation: Explicit projection limits the data returned to the caller.

questions.prompt: What should a useful audit event normally identify?
options: The subject, action, actor reference and event time
The user's plaintext password
Every secret in the row
Only the current row count
questions.answer: The subject, action, actor reference and event time
questions.explanation: Audit events should be attributable and relevant to the change.

questions.prompt: Does an audit table automatically become tamper-proof?
options: No; access, integrity and retention controls are still required
Yes, because it has a primary key
Only if it has a TEXT column
Yes, after an index is created
questions.answer: No; access, integrity and retention controls are still required
questions.explanation: Database access controls and operational processes protect audit integrity.

questions.prompt: Why write a business update and its audit row in one transaction?
options: So both changes commit or roll back together
To make the query run without indexes
To avoid checking affected rows
To expose the audit table publicly
questions.answer: So both changes commit or roll back together
questions.explanation: A single transaction helps keep the business state and audit evidence consistent.
